dq.overview: In Dragon Quest, magic is called "incantations" (jumon), and you cast them by spending MP. Sources divide them into attack incantations, support incantations (buffs and debuffs), healing incantations, and travel incantations, plus Parupunte, the "mysterious incantation" that fits none of them. Attack incantations come in families such as Mera (fireball), Gira (flash), Hyado (ice), Bagi (vacuum and whirlwind), Io (explosion), Dein (lightning), Doruma (darkness), Jibaria (ground explosion), and Dogan (rock). Each family has beginner, intermediate, advanced, and top-tier stages, and the name itself changes as the stage rises. The family system has grown along with the series. Many families took shape as stages in DQ III. The top-tier spells Meragaiā, Mahyadedosu, Iogurande, and Bagimūcho appeared from Monsters: Joker and DQ IX onward, the Doruma family from Joker onward, and Dein finally became a beginner-level spell in the main series in DQ XI. DQ X and XI also added the Jibaria family, an earth family, and DQ X Ver. 7.0 added the Dogan family. In DQ I and II the Gira family was depicted as fire or lightning, and it was later reorganized as flash. It does not appear in DQ IX. Even for the same spell, the range (single target, one group, or all enemies) often changes from game to game.
rules: The name itself changes as the stage rises (Mera -> Merami -> Merazōma -> Meragaiā)
Adding sounds such as "Be" or "Ma" can mark a stronger or wider version (Hoimi -> Behoimi, Hyado -> Mahyado, Gira -> Begirama)
A family shares a common sound (the -dein spells, Doru-, and the Za- of the Zaki family)
Each purpose has its own family of names (the Hoimi family for healing, the Zaki family for instant death, the Zao family for revival, and so on)
Names that use English as is, such as Majikkubaria, are an exception
growth: Attack incantations basically have four stages per family (beginner, intermediate, advanced, top-tier), and some games add a semi-advanced stage (such as Hyadain)
Higher stages hit harder, and in some families the target also widens from one enemy to one group to all enemies (Zaki -> Zaraki -> Zarakīma)
Some pairs use separate names for the single-target and all-target versions (Sukara/Sukuruto, Rukani/Rukanan, Piora/Piorimu)
Incantations are basically learned by leveling up, per character or per class (how they are learned differs by game)

dq1.overview: In DQ I, magic is called "incantations" (jumon). The hero is the only character who casts them, learning all 10 by leveling up and casting them with MP. He travels alone and fights one enemy at a time, so every attack and status incantation targets a single enemy, and healing incantations affect only himself. The families are still small. Healing has just two stages, Hoimi -> Behoimi, and fire (the later Gira family) has just two, Gira -> Begirama. The rest are sleep (Rarihō), spell sealing (Mahotōn), and travel incantations for light, escape, return, and warding off monsters. This is the first game in the series, so there is no earlier title, but many of the names born here were carried into later games.
rules: Names are short katakana coinages that do not carry a meaning (Hoimi, Gira, Rarihō)
Upper versions are made by adding a sound at the front (Hoimi -> Behoimi, Gira -> Begirama)
Travel incantations get the same kind of coined names (Riremito, Rūra, Toherosu, Remīra)
growth: The hero learns every incantation by leveling up, in a fixed order
Healing and attack each have two stages, and the upper version has a bigger effect and costs more MP

dq2.overview: In DQ II, only the Prince of Samaltoria and the Princess of Moonbrooke can cast incantations, and the Prince of Lorasia learns none. The Prince handles healing, support, and attack, while the Princess is good at attacks and weakening enemies, so the two have distinct roles. What changed from the previous game is that the party has three members and fights several enemies, so incantations now distinguish targets: one enemy group, all enemies, and all allies. Bagi, Ionazun, Zaraki, Megante, Behoma, Zaoriku, Sukuruto, Rukanan, Manūsa, Kiarī, Toramana, Abakamu, and Parupunte were newly added, bringing the total to 22. The families are still not organized, though. The Io family has only Ionazun and the Zaki family has only Zaraki, so spells that later became upper versions appear first.

dq3.overview: DQ III introduced the class system, and incantations split into two lines: the Mage (attack and support) and the Priest (healing and debuffs). The Sage learns both, and the Hero learns parts of both lines plus Hero-only incantations: Raidein, Gigadein, Behomazun, Asutoron, and Toherosu. The big change from the previous game is that families such as Mera, Hyado, Io, Bagi, Dein, and Zaki were organized into beginner, intermediate, and advanced stages. Lower spells, Io, Iora, and Zaki, were added to Ionazun and Zaraki, which had appeared earlier in DQ II. The number of incantations also grew a lot, from 22 in DQ II to 60, and support incantations that have separate names for single-target and all-target versions, such as Rukani, Sukara, Baikiruto, and Piorimu, were now all in place. Rūra can now take you to any town you have visited.

dq4.overview: DQ IV dropped the class system, and each character learns a fixed set of incantations by leveling up. Maya takes the Mera, Gira, and Io families, Brey the Hyado family, Kiryl and Meena healing, Meena the Bagi family, Kiryl the Zaki family, and the hero the Dein family. In other words, the Mage and Priest incantations of DQ III were distributed among the party members. Compared with DQ III, Minadein, Rarihōma, Mahosute, and Megazaru were newly added, and Abakamu, Remuoru, Bashirūra, and Shanaku and others are no longer learned by party members. Megante is used only by enemies. The incantation families and stages are almost unchanged from DQ III. In the remakes (the PlayStation version onward), the MP costs of healing and travel incantations were revised significantly.

dq5.overview: In DQ V, incantations are again learned per character by leveling up, but many of the party members are now recruited monsters, and each monster species learns its own fixed incantations. Among the human party members, the hero handles healing and the Bagi family, the bride (Bianca or Flora) handles the Mera and Gira families and support, the son handles the Dein family and healing, and the daughter handles the Io and Hyado families and support. Compared with the previous game, Mahokite was newly added, and Asutoron, Moshasu, Mahosute, and others are no longer party incantations. Hyadain disappeared, and ranges were revised: Mahyado and Raidein hit all enemies, and Medapani and Rarihōma hit one enemy group. The family stages are almost the same as in DQ III and IV, and most MP costs carry over from DQ IV.

dq6.overview: In DQ VI, incantations are cast with MP, and sources divide them into healing, attack, support (hindering), and travel. The Mera, Gira, Hyado, Bagi, Io, and Dein families line up in three stages (beginner, intermediate, advanced), and the name itself changes with each stage (Mera -> Merami -> Merazōma). In the games up to DQ V, incantations were mainly learned by party members leveling up. This game brings back class changes, and incantations can also be learned by raising a class's mastery (stars). Zarakīma, Majikkubaria, Mahotān, Furōmi, and Remirāma debuted in this game, and strong moves such as Madante and Gigaslash are classified as skills, not incantations. The Dein family is handled by the Hero class and the protagonist, and in this game Gigadein targets one enemy group. Moshasu is enemy-only.

dq7.overview: In DQ VII, incantations are cast with MP, and sources divide them into attack, healing, support, and travel. The family and stage structure is almost the same as in DQ VI, with the Mera, Gira, Hyado, Bagi, Io, and Dein families in three stages. The difference from DQ VI is that, in addition to human classes, there are monster classes in which you transform into a monster to fight. This created incantations that human classes do not learn and only monster classes do, such as Hyado, Zaki, Mahotān, and Behomazun. In the PlayStation version there are also "class history skills," learned by experiencing certain classes in combination, and Mahotora and Sukuruto are learned that way. New incantations include the pirate water spells Kōrarurein and Meirusutoromu, and the support-canceling Majasutisu and Gigajatisu, which the hero learns through events.

dq8.overview: In DQ VIII, incantations are cast with MP. Sources divide them into attack, healing, and support, and there are also travel incantations used on the field. As in DQ VII, the family stages are three: beginner, intermediate, and advanced. The class changes and mastery of earlier games are gone. The four fixed party members (the hero, Yangus, Jessica, and Angelo) learn incantations by leveling up and by putting points into skills. Some incantations, like those of the Staff skill, can be learned by both Jessica and Angelo, who share the same skill. Madante, which was a skill in earlier games, and Angelo's Gurandokurosu became incantations in this game. Medapanīma, Dibainsuperu, Pesukatore, and Mahoageru debuted here. Casting after raising your tension makes an incantation stronger.

dq9.overview: In DQ IX, incantations are cast with MP, and sources divide them into attack, healing, support, hindering, and travel. To the three stages up to advanced in DQ VIII, the top-tier spells Meragaiā, Mahyadedosu, Iogurande, and Bagimūcho were added, so many families now have four stages. The dark Doruma family, Behoimu (which sits in the middle of the Hoimi family), the single-target versions Piora, Bomie, and Bāha, Henatosu (which lowers attack power), and Mahobaria all debuted in a main-series game here as well. Meanwhile, the Gira and Dein families are gone from the incantations the player can use. Party members are not fixed characters but ones you create yourself, and incantations are learned at each class's levels and usable while you are in that class. The power of an incantation and the amount it heals change with your attack magic and healing magic stats.

dq10.overview: DQ X is an online RPG. Incantations are cast with MP, and sources divide them into attack, healing, support (buffs and debuffs), and other. As in DQ IX, incantations are learned at each class's levels, but the top-tier incantations (Meragaiā, Mahyadedosu, Iogurande, and others) are learned through each class's skills, and after casting one there is a period during which you cannot use it again. Characters move freely in battle, so targets are set not by one group or all enemies but by areas: a line (Gira family), around a targeted spot (Hyadaruko and Bagi families), or around yourself (Io family and Behomarā). The Gira family, which disappeared in DQ IX, returns as a line attack, and the top-tier Giragureido was added. There are many new incantations as well: the earth Jibaria and Dogan families, the heal-over-time Rihoimi family, Zao for revival, the poison Vere family, and Zusshīdo, which relates to shoving contests.

ff.overview: Magic in Final Fantasy V (Super Famicom version) is divided into White Magic (mainly healing and support), Black Magic (mainly attacks and status ailments), Time Magic (which manipulates time and gravity), Summon Magic (which calls espers), Blue Magic (which learns enemy moves), and others. White, Black, and Time Magic each have three spells at each of Levels 1 to 6. Attack magic marks its stage by changing the ending of the base form to -ra or -ga (Faia -> Faira -> Faiga, Kearu -> Kearura -> Kearuga), and many spells can be switched between single and all targets. In some cases -ga marks the all-target version, as in Surou -> Surouga and Heisuto -> Heisuga. Stage notation differs by game. In the Famicom version of FF I, single and all targets cannot be switched, so single-target healing has four stages (Kearu -> Kearua -> Kearuda -> Kearuga), while all-target healing is a separate line (Hīru -> Hīra -> Rahīra).

In the Famicom version of FF I, four stages are made by inserting -a and -da (Kearu -> Kearua -> Kearuda -> Kearuga)

ff1.overview: Magic in the Famicom version of Final Fantasy has two lines, White Magic and Black Magic, with four spells at each of Levels 1 to 8, for 64 in all. One character can learn only three spells per level, so you have to choose which ones to leave out. The cost is not MP but a number of uses per level. There is no single/all switching, and each spell has a fixed target, so the same effect becomes separate spells for the single-target and all-target versions (Purotesu/Purotea, Inbiji/Inbia). The way stages are formed is unusual. Single-target healing has four stages (Kearu -> Kearua -> Kearuda -> Kearuga), all-target healing goes Hīru -> Hīra -> Rahīra, and the anti-undead line gets stronger by adding sounds at the front (Dia -> Adia -> Dadia -> Gadia). Elemental attacks have three stages (Faia -> Faira -> Faiga), but the top Lightning spell is written Sangā, and the strongest non-elemental spell is written Fureā. Compared with FF V, the representative game, which uses a uniform three-stage -ra and -ga scheme and lets you switch many spells between single and all targets, neither the naming nor the handling of targets is organized yet.
rules: Elemental attacks change the ending to -ra and -ga to raise the stage (Faia -> Faira -> Faiga). Only the third stage of Lightning is "Sangā"
Single-target healing has four stages: Kearu -> Kearua -> Kearuda -> Kearuga
Some families raise the stage by adding sounds at the front (Dia -> Adia -> Dadia -> Gadia, Hīru -> Hīra -> Rahīra)

The all-target version sometimes changes the ending to -a (Purotesu -> Purotea, Inbiji -> Inbia)

ff2.overview: Magic in the Famicom version of Final Fantasy II has 20 White Magic spells and 20 Black Magic spells, 40 in all. You learn a spell by using a spell book, and the more you keep using the same spell, the higher its proficiency (Lv 1 to 16) rises, which increases its power and success rate. The game switches from the use counts of FF I to an MP system, and the MP cost equals the proficiency level, so the more a spell grows, the more each cast costs. There are no stage names like Faia -> Faira -> Faiga or Kearu -> Kearua -> Kearuda -> Kearuga from the previous game. A spell keeps a single name and gets stronger through proficiency (sources write a level after the name, as in "Kearu 8"). Almost every spell can also be switched between single and all targets, and choosing all targets spreads out the effect. Some spells keep their names but swap roles. Terepo, which was Black Magic in the previous game, becomes a White Magic escape spell, and Dejon takes over the job of going back a floor.
rules: Each spell has just one name, with no ending (-ra or -ga) to mark the stage
Strength is shown by adding the proficiency level after the name (Kearu 8, Faia 16, and so on)
Spell names are short English-style katakana, almost the same as in FF V (Faia, Kearu, Esuna)
Some spells keep the same name as before but change roles (Terepo is an escape, Kurauda is poison damage)
growth: Spells are learned by using "book of ..." items obtained from shops and treasure chests. Any character can learn them
Proficiency rises with each use, and at the maximum of Lv 16, power, success rate, the number of ailments cured, and so on increase
The MP cost equals the proficiency level (Lv 8 costs 8). Arutema's power barely grows even when its proficiency rises

ff3.overview: Magic in the Famicom version of Final Fantasy III has three lines: White Magic, Black Magic, and Summon Magic, each divided into Levels 1 to 8. White and Black have three spells per level, 48 in all, and Summon has one per level, 8 in all. Spells are items found in shops and treasure chests, and you "equip" up to three spells per level, up to the level your job can handle. The cost drops the proficiency and MP system of FF II and returns to the per-level use counts of FF I. The stage names are Kearu -> Kearura -> Kearuda -> Kearuga (FF I's "Kearua" becomes "Kearura") and Faia -> Faira -> Faiga, and the third stage of Lightning also changes from "Sangā" to "Sandaga," moving closer to the FF V pattern. Many attack and healing spells can be switched between single and all targets. The wind Earo family, Konfyu, and Heisuto are White Magic. Summon Magic has spell names such as "Esukepu" and "Aisun" that differ from the names of the summoned creatures (Chokobo, Shiva), and the effect changes depending on whether a Conjurer, Magus, or Sage uses it.
rules: Elemental attacks change the ending to -ra and -ga to raise the stage (Faia -> Faira -> Faiga, Sandā -> Sandara -> Sandaga)
Single-target healing has four stages: Kearu -> Kearura -> Kearuda -> Kearuga

Summon spells use short spell names that hint at their effect, not the name of the summoned creature (Esukepu = Chokobo, Hītora = Ifurīto, Bahamuru = Bahamūto)
growth: Spells are obtained as items, and you equip up to three per level to use them
The cost is a use count, with a set number of uses per level. Inns restore them
The top level you can use depends on your job (for example, Rangers and Magic Knights go up to White Magic Lv 3, while Devouts and Sages go up to Lv 8)

ff4.overview: Magic in the Super Famicom version of Final Fantasy IV is divided into White Magic (24 spells), Black Magic (24 spells), Summon Magic (15 spells), and the ninjutsu used by Edge (6 spells). It drops the per-level use counts of the games up to FF III and uses MP, with a fixed MP cost for each spell (Kearu 3, Faia 5, Meteo 99, and so on). There are no job changes. Each character has a fixed set of spells, such as Rosa and Porom (White), Palom (Black), Rydia (Black and Summon), and Tellah and Fusoya (both White and Black), learned through leveling up and events. The stage names are Kearu -> Kearura -> Kearuda -> Kearuga, Faia -> Faira -> Faiga, Burizado -> Burizara -> Burizaga, and Sandā -> Sandara -> Sandaga, almost the same form as FF V, the representative game (the difference is that the third stage of healing is still "Kearuda"). Many spells can be switched between single and all targets. Summon Magic drops FF III's spell names such as "Esukepu" and "Hītora," and the names of the summoned creatures, such as Chokobo and Ifurīto, become the spell names as they are.
rules: Elemental attacks change the ending to -ra and -ga to raise the stage (Faia -> Faira -> Faiga)
Single-target healing has four stages: Kearu -> Kearura -> Kearuda -> Kearuga
Summon spells use the summoned creature's name as the spell name (Shiva, Ramuu, Bahamūto)
Ninjutsu use kanji names (Katon, Suiton, Raijin, Kageshibari, Kemuridama, Bunshin)
growth: Each character has fixed spells, learned through leveling up and events
The cost is MP, with a fixed MP cost for each spell

ff6.overview: In the Super Famicom version of FF VI, you learn magic by equipping magicite, which is an esper that has changed form, winning battles, and building up each spell's learning points. Unlike FF V, where the job and ability level decided what magic you could use, anyone can learn the same spells just by equipping magicite, and the White, Black, and Time Magic divisions and the system of buying magic by level in shops are gone. Strategy guides organize the magic into Black Magic for attacks, White Magic for healing, and Gray Magic for support. The way stages are formed is the same as in the previous game, changing the ending to -ra and -ga (Faia -> Faira -> Faiga), and many spells can be switched between single and all targets. The equipped magicite can summon its esper once per battle. What corresponded to Blue Magic in the previous game became Strago-only "Lore." Arutema, Meruton, Kappā, Rireizu, and others were newly added.

In some cases -ga marks the all-target version (Surou -> Surouga, Heisuto -> Heisuga)
Revival has two stages, Reizu -> Areizu, and the state that revives you automatically is called Rireizu
Some Lore names include a number for the condition under which they work, such as "Reberu5 Desu" and "Reberu4 Furea"

Learned spells are cast by paying MP, and many can be switched between single and all targets

ff7.overview: In the PlayStation version of FF VII, you use magic from green "magic materia" set into the slots of weapons and armor. Each materia holds a group of spells from the same family (the Honō materia holds Faia, Faira, Faiga, and so on), and as the materia grows with AP and gains stars, higher spells become available. In FF VI, you learned magic by equipping magicite and could keep using it after taking it off. Here, a spell is usable only while the materia is equipped, and anyone can use the same spell right away just by swapping the materia. Stages are marked by the endings -ra and -ga as in the previous game, and Kueiku, Baio, and Gurabide, which stood alone before, now also have stages (Kueira, Baioga, Gurabira, and so on). Making a spell hit all targets is done by combining it with the All materia. Summons use red summon materia, and enemy moves are used through the command materia Enemy Skill. Many materia names are hiragana words such as Kaifuku, Reiki, Ikazuchi, and Fūin.

Spells that stood alone before also got stages (Kueiku -> Kueira -> Kueiga, Baio -> Baiora -> Baioga, Gurabide -> Gurabira -> Gurabiga)
Magic materia are named with hiragana words that express the effect (Honō, Reiki, Ikazuchi, Sosei, Fūjiru)
Summon materia carry the summoned creature's name, and the move used when summoning gets a different name (Shiva = Daiyamondo Dasuto)

ff8.overview: Magic in the PlayStation version of FF VIII has no MP. You obtain spells by "drawing" them from enemies or Draw Points, or by refining them from items, and you can stock up to 100 of each kind. Each cast uses up one from the stock, and the spells you hold also serve as material to junction to your stats through G.F. (summoned creatures). In FF VII, magic was usable only while materia was equipped. Here, you carry spells themselves as a count. Names mark stages with the endings -ra and -ga as in earlier games (Faia -> Faira -> Faiga), but only fire, cold, lightning, and healing have stages, and Kueiku, Baio, and Gurabide, which had stages in the previous game, return to standalone spells. New spells were added, such as Daburu, Toripuru, Ōra, Pein, and Meruton. Summons became a matter of calling junctioned G.F., and Blue Magic remained as Quistis's special skill.

Revival has two stages: Reizu -> Areizu
The number of times an effect applies is used directly as the name, as in "Daburu" and "Toripuru"
G.F. are called by their summoned creature names (Ketsakuwatoru, Gurasharaborasu, and others)

Casting uses up one from the stock (there is no MP)
Junctioning a G.F. lets you use the Magic command, and junctioning stocked spells to your stats makes you stronger

ff9.overview: In the PlayStation version of FF IX, each character has a fixed set of spells. Black Magic belongs to Vivi, White Magic to Garnet and Eiko, Summon Magic to Garnet (8) and Eiko (4), and Blue Magic to Quina. Spells come from "abilities" attached to weapons, armor, and the like. You can use the spell while the item is equipped, and once you build up AP in battle, you can use it even after taking the item off. In FF VIII, anyone could use magic through G.F. junctions and spent stock instead of MP. Here, the game returns to casting by paying MP. Stages are marked as in the rest of the series with the endings -ra and -ga (Faia -> Faira -> Faiga, Kearu -> Kearura -> Kearuga), and many spells can be switched between single and all targets. The power of Summon Magic changes with the number of gems you hold (opal, topaz, and so on), and Blue Magic is learned by "eating" enemies.

Summon Magic is called by the summoned creature's name, and the move used when summoning gets a different name (Shiva = Daiyamondo Dasuto)

ff10.overview: Magic in Final Fantasy X (PS2 version) is divided into White Magic for healing and support and Black Magic for attacks and absorption, and Yuna alone can use "Summon" to call aeons. You learn magic not through jobs or purchases but by activating squares on the Sphere Grid with spheres, so every character can eventually learn all the magic. Attack magic has three stages through the endings -ra and -ga, as in Faia -> Faira -> Faiga, and the four elements of fire, lightning, water, and ice line up. Unlike FF V, you cannot switch targets between single and all, and the all-target versions are separate spells such as Heisuga and Surouga. There is no Time Magic category, and Heisuto, Surou, Gurabide, and the like go under White Magic or Black Magic. Elemental defense is the Bafai family, which nullifies an elemental attack once. When you summon an aeon, you control it directly in battle.

The four elements of fire, lightning, water, and ice share the same way of forming stages (Wōta -> Wotara -> Wotaga)
All-target versions are separate spells with -ga added (Heisuga, Surouga)
Spells that nullify an element are "Ba + element name" (Bafai, Basanda, Bawota, Bakorudo)

ff11.overview: Final Fantasy XI is an online RPG, and its magic is divided by job into White Magic, Black Magic, Elemental Magic, Summoning Magic, songs, ninjutsu, Blue Magic, Geomancy, and so on (this site includes only the representative White Magic, Black Magic, and Summoning Magic). You learn spells by using "scrolls," and you can use them once your job level is high enough. The same spell can be learned by several jobs at different levels. It drops the -ra and -ga stage scheme of earlier games, and single-target attacks show strength with Roman numerals, as in Faia -> Faia II -> Faia III. "-ga" becomes the name for the area version (Kearuga, Faiga), and a still higher area attack, "-ja" (Faija), was added. Furea, Furīzu, and the like are elemental "Ancient Magic," and Furea in FF XI is Fire-element.

Travel magic adds a destination (Terepo-hora, Terepo-demu, Rikōru-jagu)

ff12.overview: Magic in Final Fantasy XII (PS2 version) is divided into White Magick for healing, Black Magick for elemental attacks, Time Magick that handles speed, time, and reflection, Green Magick for support and status ailments, Arcane Magick for darkness, absorption, and instant death, and Summon Magick for calling espers. You buy magic in shops, and those who have taken the matching license on the License Board can use it. The endings -ra and -ga mark stages as in earlier games, but healing has four stages, Kearu -> Kearura -> Kearuda -> Kearuga, and Kearura and Kearuga heal an area. Unlike FF V, you cannot switch between single and all targets, and attack magic from the middle stages up hits an area from the start. Area versions are shown with -ga (Surouga, Purotega, Sheruga). In The Zodiac Age, the game moves to a job system and the categories were reorganized (Purotesu and Sheru are White Magick, Burain and Suripuru and the like are Black Magick, Gurabide and Banishu are Time Magick, Dorein and Dekoi are Green Magick, and Ādā is Arcane Magick).

ff13.overview: Final Fantasy XIII (PS3 version) has no White Magic or Black Magic distinction and no MP, and magic is used as command abilities tied to each battle role. Ravagers handle elemental attacks, Medics handle healing, Synergists handle buffs, and Saboteurs handle debuffs and status ailments, while the non-elemental Ruin is used by Commandos. The cost is not MP but the number of ATB gauge segments, and higher spells use more segments. Attack magic marks stages with -ra and -ga as in earlier games, but the higher the stage, the more it becomes an area attack. Healing has its own arrangement: Kearu -> Kearura (area), and Kearua -> Kearuda (heals more the lower your HP is). Synergists have "-da" spells that give a big boost for a short time (Bureida, Puroteda), and Saboteurs have area versions with "-ga" (Depuroga, Surouga). Each character has one Eidolon, called at a cost of 3 TP.

Debuffs add "De" at the front to express the opposite of a buff (Depurote, Desheru), and area versions use the ending -ga (Depuroga, Deshega)
Spells that add an element to attacks are "En + element name," and elemental resistance is "Ba + element name" (Enfai, Bafai)

ff14.overview: Final Fantasy XIV is an online RPG, and its magic is a kind of action, along with abilities and the like, that you learn automatically at set levels for each job (this site includes only representative spells of White Mage, Black Mage, Summoner, and Red Mage). It drops the Roman numerals of the earlier FF XI and again marks stages with -ra, -ga, and -ja, but the usage is its own. Faira and Burizara are area attacks, while Faiga and Faija are upper versions of single-target attacks. Healing also splits roles, with Kearu -> Kearura single target and Kearuga area healing. The White Mage's attacks go Sutōn -> Sutonra -> Sutonga -> Sutonja -> Gurea -> Gureaga, with names replaced at high levels. The Black Mage alternates between fire and ice spells to switch MP and power, and the Summoner calls Kābankuru, Ifurīto, Bahamūto, and others.

smt.overview: In Shin Megami Tensei III: Nocturne, a demon's moves are treated as skills, and the magic that costs MP is divided into the elements Fire, Ice, Lightning, Force, Almighty, Expel, Death, Mind, Nerve, and Magic. Attack magic gains power as an ending is added to an element's stem (Agi, Bufu, Jio, Zan), as in Agi -> Agirao -> Agidain, and adding "Maha" at the front makes all enemies the target. Expel (the Hama family) and Death (the Mudo family) are spells that aim for instant death rather than damage, and "-on" raises the chance. For support, "-kaja" buffs allies and "-nda" debuffs enemies, and in this game both target everyone. Many ailment cures have names ending in "-di," and travel spells end in "-toma" or "-rama."
rules: Each element has its own stem (Agi = Fire, Bufu = Ice, Jio = Lightning, Zan = Force)
The ending marks the power stage (Agi -> Agirao -> Agidain, Zan -> Zanma -> Zandain)

The instant-death spells of Expel and Death have a higher chance with "-on," and "Maha" makes them hit all targets

smt1.overview: In Shin Megami Tensei (Super Famicom version), there are two kinds of magic. Humans other than the protagonist (the Heroine, the Law Hero, and the Chaos Hero) learn spells by leveling up, and allied demons have spells fixed from the start by race. A demon gains no new spells unless it is reborn through fusion, and there is no inheritance as in III and later. The system of stem plus ending for power and "Maha" for multiple targets already exists, but there are only two stages (Agi -> Agirao, Zan -> Zanma), with no "-dain." The top Force spell is Rimudōra, which has a different stem. Many names are written differently from III and later: Expel's instant death is not "Hama" but "Hanma," the all-target Ice spell is "Mahābufu," and the all-target ailment cure is "Penpatora." There are also effects unique to I and II, such as Hapiruma, which makes an enemy HAPPY, Tetoraja, which guards against Energy Drain, and Makatoranda, which drains an enemy's MP. Targets are divided finely into one, two, several, one group, and all. Attacks such as fangs and claws, and breaths, are handled separately as a demon's "special moves," not as magic.

smt2.overview: The magic of Shin Megami Tensei II (Super Famicom version) carries over almost the same system as the previous game, I. The attack magic of Fire (Agi), Ice (Bufu), Lightning (Jio), and Force (Zan) has two stages each for single targets and for multiple targets with "Maha," Almighty goes Megido -> Megidoraon, Expel's instant death is "Hanma," and Death's is "Mudo." Rimudōra, the top Force spell from I, Makatora, which shares MP, and Makatoranda, which drains MP, are gone. Demon moves are divided into magic and "special moves," and breaths, kicks, songs, and the like are special moves.

smt4.overview: In Shin Megami Tensei IV, magic is part of the "skills" that demons and the protagonist learn, and it costs MP. The elements are the attacks of Fire, Ice, Lightning, Force, and Almighty, plus Expel and Death, which aim for instant death. The stages of stem plus ending (Agi -> Agirao -> Agidain) and making spells hit all enemies with "Maha" are the same as in III, and both single and all targets have three stages. In IV FINAL, demon-specific skills such as "Shin Jiodain," "Kingubufūra," and "Megidoāku" grew greatly, and many of IV's download-only skills were dropped from the list.

smt5.overview: In Shin Megami Tensei V, magic consists of skills learned by demons and the protagonist (Nahobino), and it costs MP. The elements are Fire, Ice, Lightning, Force, Expel, Death, and Almighty. The stages of stem plus ending and making spells hit everyone with "Maha" are the same as in IV, but a fourth stage, "-barion" (Agibarion, Mahajiobarion), was added. In V Vengeance, "unique skills," automatic effects for each demon, and Magatsuhi skills used by several demons were added. New demons' exclusive skills (Megidoāku, Gei Borugu, and others) increased, and Esutoma moved from a skill to a function of "Divine Will," which uses Magatsuhi.

persona.overview: In Persona 5 Royal, every move a Persona learns is called a "skill," and magic costs SP. The instant death of the Hama and Mudo families was Light and Darkness in P3 (P3P), but in P5 they became Bless and Curse, and damage spells (the Kouha and Eiha families) were added to the same elements. Nuclear and Psychic also did not exist in P3 (P3P), and were added as elements in P5.

persona1.overview: In Megami Ibunroku Persona, magic belongs to the Persona, and a Persona learns new spells as its rank rises. Magic is divided into Spirit Magic (Fire, Ice, Wind, Quake), Physical Magic (Nuclear, Force, Gravity, Lightning), Dark Magic (Death, Nerve, Awakening, Kōma), Holy Magic (Expel, Revelation, Bless, Miracle), and Special Magic. The form of adding an ending to a stem to raise power and using "Maha" to hit all targets is the same as in later games, but "-dain" targets multiple enemies, and adding "Bai" makes a spell hit multiple targets (Baieiha). Hama is written "Hanma," and the Megido family is Nuclear rather than Almighty. The Hama and Mudo families deal damage over time in addition to instant death, and Eiha and Kouha are spells that deal damage over time through a curse or holy power. There are also many spells with unique names that pair up in the same element, such as 止揚の紅 and 終焉の碧. SP cost is set per Persona, not per spell. This is the first game in the Persona series, so there is no earlier title in the series.

persona2.overview: In Persona 2: Innocent Sin, magic belongs to Personas, and a Persona learns new spells as its rank rises. The elements are Flame, Water, Gale, Earth, Ice, Lightning, Nuclear, Almighty, Holy, and Dark, plus the status categories Nerve and Mind, which is more of a split than in Persona 3 and later. Two patterns are shared with the later games: a stem plus an ending that raises power (Akua -> Akuesu -> Akuadain), and the prefix Maha, which targets one group of enemies. In this game, however, Maha spells hit a group, not all enemies. Many spells are also unique names with no stem, such as Faiasutōmu (Fire Storm) and 雷の洗礼. Zan is an Almighty spell here, not a Force spell, and Hamaon and Mudoon target all enemies. SP cost is set per Persona, not per spell, and it goes up or down depending on how well the Persona suits the character using it. Compared with the previous game, Revelations: Persona, this game adds the Water element (the Akua family), merges Quake into Earth, and makes Zan (formerly Force), Gurai (Gravity), and the Megido family (formerly Nuclear) all Almighty. The -dain spells that hit several enemies in the previous game now hit a single target, Hanma became Hama, and fusion spells that several Personas cast together were added. Eternal Punishment adds still more unique-name spells for each element, along with spells that put up elemental barriers.

mother.overview: In Mother 2 (EarthBound), the psychic powers that serve as magic are called "PSI," and you use them by spending PP. PSI is divided into Offense, Healing, Assist, and Other. A name is a type name plus a Greek letter, and the letter marks the stage (alpha -> beta -> gamma -> omega). Only offensive PSI has "PK" in its name, while Healing and Assist do not. The number of stages differs by PSI, and many have only two, alpha and omega. In that case omega is usually the all-targets version. Shield and Psychic Shield have a sigma, which serves as the all-targets version of alpha. Notation differs by game: Mother 1 uses pi (Raifuappu π and Hīringu π) and sometimes gives the single-target and all-target versions different names (Bureinshokku / Bureinsaikuron). Mother 3 has shortened names such as Ofeappu and Difedaun.

metaphor.overview: In Metaphor: ReFantazio, magic is one of the skills each archetype (job) learns, and it uses MP. Attack magic is divided into Fire, Ice, Lightning, Wind, Light, Darkness, and Almighty. Each element has a base name (Botto, Burizu, Kande, Saiku, Hanma, Mudo), and an ending raises it through three stages, small, medium, and large. Basic attack magic targets one enemy, and the archetypes have no Maha version that hits all enemies (Mahanma, Mahamudo, and the like are Syntheses, used by combining party members). All-enemy attacks come from the Almighty Megido family, unique-name spells of higher archetypes (Tankyū no Kaze, 真紅の炎華, and so on), and the Summoner line's summoning magic (Ryūjinshōkan, Yōseishōkan, and so on). Hama and Mudo, which were instant-death spells in Megami Tensei and Persona, are Light and Darkness damage spells in this game. Healing and support carry on Megami Tensei names, including variations on the Dia family (Di -> Diama -> Diamahan) and the -kaja and -nda spells.
rules: Each element has its own base name (Botto = Fire, Burizu = Ice, Kande = Lightning, Saiku = Wind, Hanma = Light, Mudo = Darkness)
The ending marks the power stage (Botto -> Bottorā -> Boattona, Kande -> Kanderā -> Kandeon)
Healing starts with Di for a single target and Medi for all
Support uses -kaja to buff and -nda to debuff, and Maha makes it hit all
growth: Advancing to a higher archetype teaches the higher spell of the same element (for example, Magician's Botto -> Wizard's Bottorā -> Elemental Master's Boattona)
The basic line of attack magic is single-target only, and there is no all-target line
Learned skills can be inherited by other archetypes

saga1.overview: In Makai Tōshi Sa-Ga (The Final Fantasy Legend), magic is not learned. You obtain it as a magic book such as Faia no Sho or Kearu no Sho (or as a magic staff) and equip it to use it. It is equipped in the same slot as a weapon, its use count drops each time you use it, and when it runs out you can no longer use it. Power and success rate depend on Magic power. The book's name contains the spell name as is, and with few kinds the roles are divided: elemental attacks (fire, cold, electricity, poison), Furea, which hits all enemies, sleep, petrification, instant death, and HP recovery. There are no stronger versions in the same line, and no stages.
rules: The spell name plus "no sho" (book) is itself the item name
Spell names are short English-style names that express the effect, such as Faia, Burizado, and Sandā
Staffs are called by item names such as "Iyashi no Tsue" and "Majutsu no Tsue," not by spell names
growth: There is no learning or leveling of magic, and you buy replacement books in shops
Each book has a use count and disappears when it runs out
The effect depends on the user's Magic power

Books are treated as a kind of weapon, have use counts, and their effects depend on Magic power. The lineup of books (Faia, Burizado, Sandā, Kurauda, Furea, Suripuru, Bureiku, Desu, and Kearu) is almost the same as in the previous game, but numbers such as use counts differ by game. Staffs have names separate from the books, such as "Iyashi no Tsue" (heals all allies) and "Madōshi no Tsue" (instant death for all enemies).
rules: The spell name plus "no sho" is itself the item name
Spell names are short English-style names that express the effect
Staffs and books are called by item names and do not have spell names

saga3.overview: In Sa-Ga 3: Jikū no Hasha (Final Fantasy Legend III), magic is an item when you obtain it, but once you equip it you have "learned" it, and from then on you spend MP to use it. Magic is divided into three kinds, Black Magic (mostly attack), White Magic (mostly healing), and Ancient Magic (both attack and healing). Each has eight levels, and one character can learn up to three spells per level. Some spells mark a higher version with an FF-style ending, such as Burizado -> Burizaga and Kearu -> Kearura -> Kearuga. Most Ancient Magic consists of combination spells that you make from a magic stone by combining two elements. Most status ailment spells inflict the ailment when used on an enemy and cure it when used on an ally.

Status ailment spells have names close to the status name (Poizun, Sutōn, Paradi)
Many Ancient Magic spells have names like gods, Buddhist figures, and people, such as Miroku, Ashura, and Damian

rsaga.overview: In Romancing SaGa (the Super Famicom version), magic is called jutsuhō ("arts"), and it is divided into ten schools: Fire Arts, Water Arts, Earth Arts, Wind Arts, Light Arts, Dark Arts, Evil Arts, Qi Arts, Sorcery, and Illusion Arts. The schools are opposed in pairs, Fire and Water, Earth and Wind, Light and Dark, Evil and Qi, and Sorcery and Illusion, and you can master only one of an opposing pair. You normally buy arts at a jutsuhō shop to learn them, but Dark Arts and Evil Arts cannot be bought in shops. Each school lists a few attack, healing, and support arts, and the names mix English names that describe the effect, such as Faiabōru and Raitoningu, with kanji names such as Hi no Tori, Wanryokuhō, and Suimujutsu. There is no rule of changing a name within a school to mark stages.
rules: The mood of the names differs by school (Fire and Light Arts use English names, Qi Arts use "-hō," and Illusion Arts use "-jutsu")
Many names state the effect directly (Faiawōru, Hīruraito, Poizungasu)
There are no endings that mark stages, and each art has its own independent name

You can learn only one of two opposing schools
Arts are lined up by school, and the more costly an art, the stronger it is

sf.overview: In SaGa Frontier, magic is called jutsu ("arts"), and you use it by spending JP. Yang and Yin, Arcane and Seal, Time and Space, and Mind and Evil are opposed, and one character can hold only one of each pair. Some arts can be bought in shops, and there are higher arts that a character with the "aptitude" for that type invents during battle. Each type has a clear naming direction. Arcane Arts are named for tarot cards (sword, cup, Shinigami, tower), Seal Arts are called "-no Rūn," and Mind Arts take two kanji (Kokki, Jubaku, Kakusei).

rsaga2.overview: In Romancing SaGa 2 (the Super Famicom version), arts are divided into six schools, Fire, Water, Earth, Wind, Heaven, and Underworld Arts, and there are also combination arts that merge two schools. You learn arts at the arts research institute that the emperor builds (the Underworld Arts research institute for Underworld Arts), and new arts unlock as the master level of each school rises. Combination arts are developed by paying for research, and they are completed as the years go by. The cost is JP (Jutsu Points). Compared with the previous game, Romancing SaGa, the ten schools were reorganized into six, the method of buying arts one at a time at a jutsuhō shop changed to learning them in stages by master level, MP became JP, and combination arts that cross two schools were added. Names mix English names (Faiābōru, Gyarakushi) with kanji names (Kongōriki, Seimei no Mizu), and some names from the previous game carry over, such as Serufubāningu, Āsuhīru, and Herufaia.

rsaga3.overview: In Romancing SaGa 3 (the Super Famicom version), arts are divided into Heaven Arts (Sun and Moon) and Earth Arts (Vermilion Bird, Genbu, White Tiger, and Azure Dragon), and one person can hold one kind from Heaven Arts and up to one kind from Earth Arts. The four Earth Arts kinds carry the names of the Four Gods, and each corresponds to one of the four demon nobles (Aunas, Forneus, Arakes, and Byunei). You pay an arts master in various places to learn a school, and then buy more arts one at a time. Each school has seven arts. The top art of the Earth Arts is taught in Lance after you defeat the phantom of the demon noble, and some of the higher Sun and Moon arts can be learned only from a master in the east. The cost is JP. Compared with the previous game, Romancing SaGa (ten schools bought at a jutsuhō shop, with MP as the cost), the schools were narrowed to six and combined in a two-track structure of Heaven and Earth. The solo combination arts of Romancing SaGa 2 are gone, and combination arts are now unleashed by several people forming a formation. Serufubāningu, Seimei no Mizu, Āsuhīru, Rivaiva, Kuikkutaimu, and Shadousābanto, among others, carry over names from earlier games.

sf2.overview: In SaGa Frontier 2, magic is called jutsu ("arts"), and you use it by spending JP. Arts draw out the power of "Anima" that dwells in equipment or in a place, and they are divided into six kinds to match the Anima types: Tree Arts, Stone Arts, Fire Arts, Water Arts, Sound Arts, and Beast Arts. There are "basic arts" that use one Anima (Tree, Stone, Fire, Water, Sound, Beast) and "combination arts" that combine several Anima (Busshufaia = Tree + Fire, Shōrai = Water + Sound, and so on), and a combination art falls under the type of the first Anima. A basic art changes its name with the type of weapon (a Fire art used with a sword is "Honō no Tachi," and with a bow it is "Hiya"), and these are called art techniques. In the previous game, SaGa Frontier, you bought arts in shops or invented them from aptitude, and opposed types such as Yang and Yin could not both be held. This game has neither shops that sell arts nor opposed types. You learn arts through combination, by combining Anima commands in a Duel, or through learning after you use an Anima in battle, and to use one you need all of the matching Anima. Gustave, who has no Anima, cannot use arts.

chrono.overview: In Chrono Trigger, magic is not a separate command. It is treated as part of the "Techs" each character learns with Tech Points. In the Tech list, the techs marked with a star are magic, and you must meet Spekkio to learn magic. There are four elements, Lightning (Heaven), Shadow, Fire, and Water, and ice magic (Aisu) is included in the Water element. Adding "ga" to the base name marks a higher version that hits all enemies (Faia -> Faiga, Aisu -> Aisuga, Wōtā -> Wōtaga). Each character's elements are fixed: Crono has Lightning, Marle has Water and healing, Lucca has Fire, Frog has Water and healing, and Magus uses Shadow and all elements.

wiz.overview: The spells of Wizardry (#1, Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord) are divided into two lines, Mage spells and Priest spells, each with a few spells at each of Levels 1 to 7. Mage spells center on attacks, weakening enemies, exploration, and teleportation. Priest spells center on healing, cures, revival, and defense, and they also include attacks through words of cursing. Spell names are original coinages made by combining letters of the alphabet, so it is hard to guess an effect from a name. The katakana spellings vary by version (Ratsumapikku / Ratyumapikku, Mazopikku / Masopikku, and so on), and this site uses the spellings of the Famicom version as its standard.
rules: Every spell name is an original coinage made by combining letters (HALITO, DIOS, TILTOWAIT, and so on)
In some cases a prefix is added to the same stem to make a higher version (Harito -> Maharito -> Raharito, Sopikku -> Mazopikku, Mōrisu -> Mamōrisu)
Healing and attack have paired word forms (Diosu / Badiosu, Diaru / Badiaru, Diaruma / Badiaruma)
In some cases lengthening the ending makes a higher version (Diosu -> Diaru -> Diaruma)

bof.overview: In Breath of Fire: Ryū no Senshi, magic spends AP. Attack magic has its own stem for each line, such as fire, lightning, ice, earth, and explosion, and it grows stronger through changes in the ending or prefix, as in Padamu -> Padāma -> Padamēma. However, how the word changes varies from line to line, and some, like Padorāmu and Paenda, change shape greatly from the same beginning. Healing has the Ririfu line (Ririfu -> Apurifu -> Topurifu -> Rifuru) and revival has the Ribaru line, so each purpose also has its own line of names. Another feature is attacks that work only on the undead (the Desupu line).

In some cases adding "Mi" makes a spell hit all (Katekuto -> Mikatekuto)

bof2.overview: In Breath of Fire II: Shimei no Ko, you use magic from the battle command "Tokunō" (special ability), and it spends AP. Characters learn magic at set levels, and some is learned through events. Most of the names carry over from the previous game, and the Padamu family of fire, the Reiga family of ice, the Baru family of lightning, the Mega family of non-elemental, the Ririfu family of healing, the Ribaru family of revival, and the Katekuto family of defense boosts all return. The difference from the previous game is that each line was tidied into two or three stages. Middle stages such as Rei, Sūrei, Barura, and Maga are gone, and Reiga, which was the second stage before, and Gadabureda and Domega, which were the top stages, are now the entry point or the only spell. New additions are the Shēza family of wind, Kirie, which wipes out the undead, Yakurifu, which cures ailments all at once, Sutōru, Deiru, and Dāru, which lower enemy stats, and Pepōpa, which seals magic.

Spells that lower enemy stats are all short words (Sutōru, Deiru, Dāru)

bof3.overview: In Breath of Fire III, magic spends AP, and each character learns it at set levels. Separately, there are techniques learned by seeing an enemy's move (mikiri) and techniques learned by becoming a master's pupil, and both are swapped in as skills. Magic names carry over almost unchanged from the previous two games, and the Padamu, Reiga, Baru, Shēza, Mega, Ririfu, Ribaru, and Katekuto families are all present. The changes from II are that the AP cost of attack and support magic dropped to about half or less (healing is about the same), that Padorāmu became Padorāma and Deiru became Diru in spelling, that Baruharā became a single-target spell, and that Domega became two elements, fire and wind. New additions are the non-elemental Mekomu, Nemuri for sleep, and Powan for confusion. Character-specific moves such as Peco's breath and Momo's Shikibetsu and Uranai also appear in the magic list. Some skills also have names with the same word forms as magic, such as Pamu, Yapurifu, and Takurema.
rules: The stems of the first game carry over (fire = Pada, lightning = Baru, ice = Rei, healing = Rifu, revival = Ribaru)
A change in the ending marks the stage (Padamu -> Padāma -> Padorāma, Baru -> Babaru -> Baruharā)
Adding "Mi" makes a spell hit all (Katekuto -> Mikatekuto)

bof4.overview: In Breath of Fire IV, the abilities each character learns by level are treated as magic and use AP. They are separate from the "skills" learned from lore masters and enemies. Attack magic is divided into four elements, Fire, Wind, Water, and Earth, and each has a three-stage line (Padamu -> Padāma -> Padorāmu, Shīza -> Shēza -> Shezāga, and so on). It carries over many names from the first game, Breath of Fire: Ryū no Senshi, such as Padamu, Reiga, Bureda, Ririfu, Ribaru, and Katekuto, but the way elements are assigned has changed. The lightning Baru line and the explosion Mega line of the first game are no longer individual spells, and instead appear as combination combos that trigger when two elemental spells hit in succession (Fire + Wind gives Mega, Wind + Water gives Baru). The wind Shīza line is a new line, and the ice Rei line now has the element Water. In the first game, Dīsu handled attacks and Nina handled healing and support almost single-handedly, but in IV the users are split by element: Ursula for Fire, Nina for Wind, Scias for Water, and Cray for Earth.

bof5.overview: In Breath of Fire: Dragon Quarter, magic is not learned by level but is a kind of "skill." You obtain skills from treasure chests, enemies, and shops, and use them by threading (slotting) them onto a weapon. Only Nina can use magic skills. Skills come in Lv 1 to 3, with AP costs of 10, 20, and 30 in that order, and using them in succession makes a combo. It carries over many names from the first game, Breath of Fire: Ryū no Senshi, such as Padamu, Baru, Reiga, Gureigoru, and Wāsu, and also has names used in IV, such as Kirie, Sutōru, and Dāru. The biggest difference from Ryū no Senshi is the use of position and range on the field. Besides attack magic that hits an area such as a circle around the target point, a straight line, or a fan-shaped spread, magic circles were added that you place on the ground and that trigger when an enemy touches them (Guran- spells, -bōru spells, Mirage bombs, and so on). Healing and revival magic are gone, and healing is done by items alone.

knightgundam2.overview: In Knight Gundam Monogatari 2: Hikari no Kishi, magic that spends MP is divided into four lines, attack, healing, support, and travel. goemon.overview: In Ganbare Goemon Gaiden: Kieta Ōgon Kiseru, what corresponds to magic is called "ninjutsu" (arts), and you cast it by spending the "ninjutsu" stat. Goemon cannot use ninjutsu, and the users are Ebisumaru, Kobanneko, and Yae-chan. The names are comical hiragana and katakana sound effects and wordplay (Gororin, Nenkorori, Supīda!), and adding "Do" to the front makes a higher version that hits all and is stronger (Kaen -> Dokaen, Suisui -> Dosuisui).

kh.overview: Magic in Kingdom Hearts (the first game) has seven lines: Faia, Burizado, Sandā, Kearu, Earo, Gurabide, and Sutoppu. In the sources, Faia, Burizado, and Sandā are divided into Standard magic, Kearu and Earo into Defense magic, and Gurabide and Sutoppu into Advanced magic. Each time you obtain the "power of" a line through the story or by defeating a boss, that line is strengthened by one stage, and as in FF the names mark the stage with the endings "-ra" and "-ga." Only the Sutoppu line is shortened, as in Sutoppu -> Sutopura -> Sutopuga. Power and duration depend on your maximum MP. Summon magic is a separate command, and it becomes usable when you show the summon gems found in each world to the Fairy Godmother, calling six Disney characters such as Simba and Genie.

The Sutoppu line is shortened (Sutoppu -> Sutopura -> Sutopuga)
Made of 7 lines times 3 stages

Strengthening does not change the MP cost, and power depends on maximum MP

nier.overview: In NieR Replicant, the hero Nier can use magic only while he is with the talking book, the White Book. Magic is a black power that takes forms such as bullets, spears, and hands. Every name takes the unified form "Kuro no ..." (Black ...). It spends MP, and the effect changes with how you use it: pressing the button once, holding to charge, or releasing after charging. Besides attack magic, there are spells that block or reflect enemy magic bullets.

There are no named stages (no stronger versions)

seiken2.overview: Magic in Secret of Mana works by borrowing the power of eight spirits who join you during the journey (Undine, Gnome, Jinn, Salamander, Shade, Luna, Dryad, and Will-o'-the-Wisp). For each spirit, Primm and Popoi learn three different spells each, with Primm handling healing and support and Popoi handling attack and debuffs. Shade is for Popoi only, and Will-o'-the-Wisp is for Primm only. Spell names are English-style katakana words such as "Aisuseibā," "Hīruwōtā," and "Ekusupurōdo," and there are no higher versions of the same spell. Instead, spells grow stronger through each spirit's magic level, which rises as you use it. The previous game, Final Fantasy Adventure, had magic with the same names as FF, such as Kearu, Faia, and Burizado, but from this game on it changed to a spirit system with names of its own. Many spells can be set to single target or all targets.
rules: Spells are grouped by spirit, and Primm and Popoi each learn three from one spirit

Spells that give a weapon an element are unified as "-seibā" (Aisuseibā, Fureimuseibā, Mūnseibā)
There are no stage names such as "-ra" or "-ga" for higher versions of the same effect

As you use magic, each spirit's magic level rises, and the power and effect grow stronger
Many spells can be switched between single target and all targets

seiken3.overview: In Trials of Mana, each of the six heroes chooses the path of light or darkness through a class change, and the magic each class can use is fixed. Angela handles attack magic, Charlotte handles healing and summoning, Duran and Charlotte handle the "-seibā" spells that give a weapon an element, Riesz handles stat boosts and drops and summoning, and Hawkeye handles ninjutsu, traps, and projectiles. Magic is divided by the elements of the eight spirits (Light, Darkness, Earth, Wind, Water, Fire, Moon, and Tree), and attack magic has three stages, low, mid, and high, as in Faiabōru -> Ekusupurōdo -> Bureizuwōru. In the previous game, Secret of Mana, Primm and Popoi strengthened the same spells by using them for each spirit, but this game has no magic levels, and the class and stats (Intelligence, Spirit, and so on) decide which spells you learn and whether you can choose single or all targets. It carries over many names from the previous game, such as Faiabōru, Ekusupurōdo, and the -seibā line.

makamaka.overview: In Maka Maka, what corresponds to magic is called "transformation moves." When each of the eight party members has a medium teach them their past life, they can transform into their past-life form in battle and use moves, and each use spends TP (the equivalent of MP). The past-life forms differ by person. The hero is Prince Sharumu of the Shabashaba tribe, the girlfriend is Princess Remia of the Nyabanyaba tribe, Masa is the samurai Kyōshirō, Shinshia is the female sumo wrestler Chiyo no Hime, and Maikeru is the gangster Bitō Koruneōre. Every move is unique to one person and is learned upon reaching a set level (only Mitchī's Ai no Kunekune is learned through an event in the past-life world). Because there is no shared spell system, even moves with the same job have different names for different people (healing is Hīru, Kaifukunochie, and Kizunaoshi, and escape is Terepōto, Dasshutsunochie, and Terepōtopawā). Many moves come in sets of three of the same form, and the later one you learn, the greater its power and TP cost. There are four elements, Heat, Cold, Electricity, and Mind, and sword, sumo, and gun moves are non-elemental. There is a bug that effectively lets only the hero's moves be used while traveling. Because there are no other games in the series, there are no differences from a previous game.
rules: Move names match the job or race of the past-life form (the samurai Kyōshirō uses "-gaeshi" and "-giri," the female sumo wrestler Chiyo no Hime uses "Tsuppari," "Kamashi," and "Shikofumi," the nurse Nasutāsha uses "-naoshi," "-no teate," and "-no chiryō," and the philosopher Kirakudesu uses "-no jikken," "-no chie," and "-bue")
The moves of the prince, the princess, and Uruuru Kingu have English-style katakana names (Aisu, Faiyābōru, Fotonburō), while the other party members mostly have hiragana names
Stages of strength are marked by a word at the front (Tsuppari -> Ootsuppari -> Toripurutsuppari, Kamashi -> Buchikamashi -> Bukkamashi, Dōpingu -> Sūpādōpin -> Haipādōpin)
Effects of the same kind share an ending (Heroherobīmu, Funyarakabīmu, Noronorobīmu; Faitoippatsu, Gādoippatsu, Dasshuippatsu)
Cure moves have names that play on words for "cured" and "vanishing" (Kazenaōru, Tachinaōru, Dokukiēru)
growth: When a medium teaches you a past life you can transform, and after that you learn set moves by leveling up
Many moves come in sets of three, and the later one you learn, the greater its power and TP cost
There are separate sets for single target, group, and all targets (the Aisu line and the Furīzā line, the Hottobōru line and the Kaen line, the Purazumasupāku line and the Atomikkuburō line)
Mitchī's support moves include the single-target "-ippatsu" and the all-target "-renpatsu"

tales.overview: In Tales of Phantasia, what corresponds to magic is called "jutsu" (arts), and it spends TP and takes effect after you chant the spell. The collective name for these arts together with the physical moves of sword and bow (special moves, mystic arts, and so on) is "jutsugi." Arts come in three kinds by user. Arche's "magic" (majutsu) is attack arts that use the mana in the air, and she learns them by buying or finding spellbooks. Mint's "holy arts" (hōjutsu) are healing and support arts, learned by leveling up. Klarth's "summoning arts" use a pact ring to make a contract with a spirit and call it to attack. The names are mostly English written in katakana. Because it is the first game in the series, there is no previous game, but in the PlayStation version the arts were swapped from the original Super Famicom version (Faiawōru, Desukuraudo, Heisuto, and others disappeared, and Sutōnburasuto, Bigguban, Chāji, Taimusutoppu, Purūto, and others were added), and the TP costs were also revised. In later games the name for arts changes: Destiny calls them Shōjutsu (晶術), Innocence calls them Tenjutsu (天術), and Xillia calls them Seireijutsu (精霊術).
rules: The names of majutsu and hōjutsu are English written in katakana (Faiabōru, Aisunīdoru, Hīru, Rikabā, Bariā)

Majutsu names include a word that fits the element (fire has Faia-, Irapushon, and Ekusupurōdo, water has Aisu-, Meirusutorōmu, and Taidaruwēbu, wind has Sutōmu, Saikuron, and Tenpesuto, and earth has Sutōn-, Rokku-, and Āsukeiku)
For summoning arts, the name of the spirit being called is itself the name of the art (Shirufu, Undīne, Ifurīto, Orijin)
In some cases, words are piled up to mark a wider version, as with Pikohan and Pikopikohanmā

The name for arts as a whole changes by game. This game calls majutsu, hōjutsu, and summoning arts together "jutsu," Destiny and Destiny 2 call them Shōjutsu (晶術), Eternia calls them Shōreijutsu (晶霊術), Rebirth calls them Dōjutsu (導術), Jinjutsu (陣術), and Renjutsu (錬術), Innocence calls them Tenjutsu (天術), Legendia calls them Sōjutsu (爪術), Xillia calls them Seireijutsu (精霊術), Zestiria calls them Tenkyōjutsu (天響術), and Berseria calls them Seireijutsu (聖隷術)
growth: Majutsu is learned by buying a spellbook at a shop, finding one in a chest or bookshelf, or receiving one in an event (some are found in different places in the past and the future)
Hōjutsu is learned in a set order as Mint's level rises (from Pikohan at LV5 to Taimusutoppu at LV53)
Summoning arts become usable when you go to a spirit with the pact ring and make a contract
There are no stage endings such as "-ra" or "-ga," and strength is divided by TP cost and breadth of range

kiseki.overview: In Trails in the Sky FC, magic is called "Arts" (Arts, orbal magic). Characters carry an orbal device called an Orbment, and use it by setting quartz (crystal circuits made from sepith, fragments of the seven-colored septium) into its six slots. Quartz carries attribute values for the seven septium elements, Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Time, Space, and Mirage, and when the total of the attribute values on the lines connecting the slots reaches the attribute values an art requires, that art becomes usable. There is no system of learning by level and no class-specific magic, and which arts who can use depends on how the quartz is arranged and the shape of the lines. Using one spends EP, and there is a wait (driving) until the casting finishes. "Crafts" and "S-Crafts," in which you fight with swords or martial arts, are a separate category of moves that use CP, and they are not included in Arts. Because this is the first game in the Trails series, there is no previous game in the same series, and names that appear here, such as Tia and Faiaboruto, carry on in later games. There are no Space-attribute attack arts yet, and the Mirage attribute has only two, confusion and a stat boost.

The area version takes "Ra" in front (Ra Tia, Ra Tiara, Ra Kyuria) or "Ōru" at the end (Anchiseputoōru)
The strengthened version adds "Kai" after the name (Faiaboruto Kai, Kurokkuappu Kai)
Attack art names are English-style katakana words that include a word for the element (Sutōn and Āsu, Akua and Burū, Faia and Furea, Ea and Earo)
growth: Arts are not learned by level. They become usable when the total attribute values of the quartz on the same line reach the required attribute values
The higher the art, the larger the required attribute values, and some require a combination of several elements (Borukanikkureibu needs Fire 8, Earth 4, and Space 2)
Slots are opened with sepith, and quartz is also made from sepith. The longer a character's lines, the easier it is to use higher arts

suikoden.overview: In Suikoden, magic is used through the power of "Runes." When a rune master has a sealing sphere placed in you, you can use the four spells fixed to that rune (Levels 1 to 4), and there is no system of learning individual spells. Which level you can use and how many times you can use each level are decided by the character's growth in "Magic." The runes include the five basic types, Fire, Water, Wind, Earth, and Lightning, their higher forms, Blazing Fire, Flowing Water, Whirlwind, Great Earth, and Thunderclap, and the Exorcism Rune (Hama), which has healing and holy attacks. A higher rune moves the Level 2 to 4 spells of the lower rune up to Levels 1 to 3 and adds one new spell at Level 4. Only the True Rune Soul Eater that the hero holds levels up as the story progresses. Because it is the first game in the series, there is no previous game.

Healing spells include words of tenderness such as "yasashisa" and "iyashi" (Yasashikishizuku, Yasashisa no Mizu, Iyashi no Kaze)
Stronger and weaker versions of the same type are marked by adding words (Ikari no Ichigeki -> Gekido no Ichigeki)
The Exorcism Rune is built from words of scolding and encouraging people: Kogoto, Kiai, Katsu, and Hama
Soul Eater has names that suggest death and the underworld, such as Shi no Yubisaki, Meifu, and Sabaki

A higher rune (Blazing Fire, Flowing Water, Whirlwind, Great Earth, Thunderclap) has the lower rune's Level 2 to 4 spells at Levels 1 to 3 and adds one new spell at Level 4

goldensun.overview: In Golden Sun: The Lost Age, the power that corresponds to magic is called "Energy" (enajī, Psynergy in the English version), and using it spends EP (Energy Points). Energy is divided into four elements, Earth (Venus), Water (Mercury), Fire (Mars), and Wind (Jupiter). The Energy you learn is decided by your level and your "class," and the class changes depending on which Djinn (spirits with an element) you set on whom and how many. Stacking Djinn of the character's own element gives a higher class in the same line (for Isaac, Swordsman -> Knight -> Swordmaster), while combining Djinn of other elements gives different classes such as Mercenary, Ninja, and Samurai, and the whole lineup of usable Energy is swapped out. Many attack Energies are three-stage lines, and the effective range (1, 3, 5, or 7 enemies) makes the effect bigger on the enemy in the center. Besides battle Energy, there is puzzle Energy that moves rocks and pillars in the field, such as Mūbu and Rifuto, and Supin, Chirudo, Gurou, and Akua can be used in both battle and puzzles. Summoning calls a spirit using 1 to 4 Djinn in Standby, and the more you use, the stronger the spirit. Because this is the first game in the series, there is no difference from a previous game.
rules: In a three-stage line, adding words to the base name makes it stronger (Kueiku -> Āsukueiku -> Kueikusufia, Purai -> Puraiweru -> Ānesutopurai)
Support Energy for one person and for everyone is separated by adding "Hai" (Inpakuto -> Haiinpakuto, Rejisuto -> Hairejisuto). Only Daru is doubled as "Darudaru"
Ninja moves are "-no jutsu" (Bakuen no Jutsu, Raijin no Jutsu), and Samurai moves have Japanese-style hiragana names (Masekigan, Onikazan, Shugobosatsu)
Puzzle Energy uses short katakana words that state the action as is (Mūbu, Rifuto, Kyatchi, Kyarī, Sutoppu)
Summons use the names of mythical gods and spirits, and the summon from one Djinn uses the name of the planet for the element (Vīnasu, Mākyurī, Māzu, Jupitā)
growth: As you level up, you learn the Energy set by your current class
When you swap Djinn and the class changes, the usable Energy is swapped to match the class (a higher class in the same line learns higher stages sooner)
For summoning, the spirit you can call changes with the number of Djinn in Standby (1 to 4), and the user's power of that element rises
Some puzzle Energy becomes usable by whoever equips an item

rudra.overview: Magic in Treasure of the Rudras is "kotodama" (word-spirits), which the player makes by lining up up to six katakana characters in the "Create" menu. Any string of characters has some effect, and even one character becomes a kotodama. The entered string is broken into dictionary words from the end, and the last word (the root word) decides the element and basic effect, while the words before it (prefixes) decide the increase or decrease in power, MP cost, and range. The basic attack words are seven: Fire Igu, Water Aku, Lightning Tou, Wind Teo, Sun Soa, Moon Sere, and None Nihi. Adding rank words (Na, Rusu, Muru, Tōmu, and so on) makes them stronger in six stages, and each has a single-target version and a multi-target version. Only the Earth element has its stages split by unique words, Rato, Rebu, and Men, and Pura, Purāto, and Puratāna. Healing is the Refu line, and there are also support kotodama for stat control, status changes, instant death, vanishing, absorption, and escape. You can learn kotodama from townspeople, chests, and moves enemies use, and entering the names of other games' healing spells, such as "Hoimi," "Kearu," and "Dia," also gives a healing effect. It is not part of a series, so there is no previous game.
rules: Attack kotodama begin with a two-character base word for each element (Igu = Fire, Aku = Water, Tou = Lightning, Teo = Wind, Soa = Sun, Sere = Moon, Nihi = None)

After the base word comes a word marking the rank (Na, Rusu, Muru, Tōmu, Rande, Rekusu, Natēsu, Tīo, Tiumu), and the Rāmuru and Gurannna ranks are sandwiched front and back as "Rā + base word + muru" and "Guran + base word + na"

The same effect has several names (synonyms), and attack kotodama of the Tōmu rank and above have two-character alternate names such as Kau, Nebu, and Jin. Adding prefixes to these short names makes good use of the six-character limit

Many support kotodama have names that include the sound of an element, like the "-riro-" status change line (Irirogu = burn, Ariroku = freeze, Torirou = shock, Teriroo = levitation, Soriroa = auto-heal, Nirirohi = berserk)

Many words are plays on the spell names of other games (Meha = Zameha, Furamu = Nifuramu, and so on), and entering "Hoimi," "Kearu," or "Dia" gives a healing effect (the word itself is not registered, but the combination of the words it breaks into produces it)
growth: Rank words make a kotodama of the same element stronger in six stages. The higher the stage, the higher the base power (10 -> 20 -> 35 -> 55 -> 80 -> 110) and MP cost, and each stage has a single-target version and a multi-target version (all enemies, 0.75 times the power)

Putting a prefix in front raises power and MP cost. The size of the increase is set for each word (Konto is small, Mō is large, and so on), and stacking adds up, but stacking the same word halves the effect step by step

There are words such as "Ko" and "Pe" that raise power while lowering MP, words such as "Ti" that lower power and MP greatly, and words that change range such as "Wo" (single target) and "Na" and "Ma" (multi-target), so depending on the combination you can even make a high-power kotodama that costs 1 MP
Using a word of another element as a prefix changes the element and range, and stacking opposite elements (Fire and Water, Lightning and Wind, Sun and Moon) lowers the power

phantasystar.overview: In Phantasy Star II, the power that corresponds to magic is called "Techniques," and you use it by spending TP (Technique Points). Seven of the eight party members, all but Rudogā, who cannot use Techniques, learn them at set levels, and the kinds they learn differ greatly by person (Annu handles healing and support, Hyūi handles those for biological enemies, and Kainzu handles those for mechanical enemies). Strategy guides divide them into six groups: attack, healing, support, anti-biological, anti-mechanical, and other. Its feature is that a base word such as Foie (fire), Zan (wind), or Resuta (healing) takes a prefix to mark the stage or range: "Gi" is mid-level, "Na" is high-level, and "Sa" is a version that widens the target to several, combined as in Saresuta -> Gisaresuta -> Nasaresuta. In the previous game, Phantasy Star, magic was called "Magic" and was cast with MP, and names such as Hīru / Dohīru, Fureeri, and Tandore were all over the place, with no system of stages by prefix.
rules: The base word is the name of the line (Foie = fire, Zan = wind, Gurantsu = light, Gurabuto = gravity, Resuta = healing, Gāji = damage to mechanical enemies)
The prefix "Gi" makes mid-level and "Na" makes high-level (Foie -> Gifoie -> Nafoie, Resuta -> Giresuta -> Naresuta)
The prefix "Sa" widens the target to all enemies, all allies, and so on (Resuta -> Saresuta, Shūtsu -> Sashūtsu, Gāji -> Sagāji, Boruto -> Saboruto)
Prefixes are stacked (Gi + Sa = Gisaresuta, Na + Sa = Nasagāji). As an exception, Sākura, whose word already begins with "Sa," takes "Na" to become the all-allies version, Nasākura
There are pairs for biological and mechanical enemies that change only the ending (the paralysis Rimita / Rimite)
growth: A line basically has three stages, base, Gi, and Na, and the higher the stage, the higher the power or healing amount and the TP cost (Foie TP 2 -> Gifoie TP 6 -> Nafoie TP 12)
The Sa lines with widened range also have the same three stages (Saresuta, Gisaresuta, Nasaresuta; Sagāji, Gisagāji, Nasagāji)

Techniques are learned by each character at set levels, and even the same Technique is learned at different levels by different people (Gifoie is Lv 5 for Yūshisu, Lv 12 for Hyūi, and Lv 15 for Shiruka)
Only Mushika is not learned by level but taught in town for money

shiningforce.overview: Shining Force: Kamigami no Isan is a simulation RPG fought on a grid battlefield, and magic is an action that uses MP, chosen alongside the normal attack. Each kind of magic has up to four levels, and you choose the level when you use it. As the level rises, the MP cost increases, and the power, range, and area of effect (1 square, 5 squares in a cross, 13 squares) widen. Many attack spells return to a 1-square area at Lv 4, and in exchange deal big damage. The magic and levels each character learns are fixed. The mages (Tao, Anri, and Arefu) handle attack and disruption, the priests (Rou, Chippu, and Tōrasu) and the monk Gongu handle healing and support, and the magical creature Domingo, the shinobi Hanzō, and the knight Ākutā also use some. The names are English-style katakana words (Bureizu, Furīzu, Supāku, Hīru, Ōra). The previous game, Shining in the Darkness, was also a dungeon RPG with a three-person party in which many spells had levels, but this game has a large force of units and a tactical system in which the number of squares of range and area changes with the level.
rules: They are English-style katakana words that use the element or effect as the name as is (Bureizu, Furīzu, Supāku, Surīpu)
Strength is shown by level (Lv 1 to 4) without changing the name (Hīru 1 to Hīru 4)
Raising and lowering stats uses paired English words (Kuikku / Surou)
Defense and disruption spells use compound words such as "Anchi-" and "-worū" (Anchisuperu, Anchidoute, Superuworu)
growth: Each kind of magic goes up to Lv 4. As a character levels up, they learn the next level of magic at set levels
You choose the Lv when you use it, and the higher the Lv, the more MP cost, power, range, and area of effect (1 square -> 5 squares in a cross -> 13 squares)
Lv 4 of attack magic returns the area to a single target and deals big damage to one target
How high a Lv each character learns differs (Ōra Lv 4 only for Tōrasu, Supāku Lv 4 only for Arefu)

categories.desc: Attack magic (Bureizu, Furīzu, Supāku), instant death, disruption such as sleep and magic sealing, and attack up

categories.name: Priest magic
categories.desc: Healing (Hīru, Ōra), antidote, raising and lowering speed, and a guard against magic

categories.name: Other

pokemon.overview: In Pokémon Red & Green, every action a Pokémon uses in battle is called a "move" (waza). The game has no category called "magic," and strikes such as a tackle and fire or psychic power are all treated as the same "moves." Every move has one of 15 "types," and each move spends a set number of uses (PP). One Pokémon can learn up to four, learned through level-ups, Technical Machines (TMs), and Hidden Machines (HMs). In the first generation, whether a move is physical or special is decided by its type, and the attack moves of Fire, Water, Grass, Electric, Ice, Psychic, and Dragon are special moves, whose power and defense are both decided by the "Special" stat. This site includes these special moves, and the support, healing, and status ailment moves with no power, as the equivalent of magic. Names mix everyday hiragana words (Hinoko, Nemuru) with katakana words (Haidoroponpu), and there are no fixed endings or prefixes that mark stages. Because it is the first game in the series, there is no previous game.
rules: Move names use everyday hiragana words (Hinoko, Awa, Utau), katakana words (Haidoroponpu, Sōrābīmu), and mixtures of them (10 Manboruto, Reitoubīmu)
Names state the phenomenon or action as is, and there are no coined spell-like words
There is no rule (ending or prefix) that makes weak and strong moves share a name form
Even for the same effect, there are names that suit the Pokémon using them (Nemurigona, Utau, Saiminjutsu, Akuma no Kissu, and Kinoko no Houshi are all moves that put the target to sleep)
growth: By leveling up, each kind of Pokémon learns set moves at set levels
Using a TM (one time only) or an HM (any number of times), you teach a move to a Pokémon that can learn it
A Pokémon can know up to four moves, and to learn a new one it must forget an old one
Within the same type, the higher a move's power, the lower its PP, and some have low accuracy (Hinoko PP 25, power 40; Daimonji PP 5, power 120, accuracy 85)

categories.desc: Attack moves of Fire, Water, Grass, Electric, Ice, Psychic, and Dragon. Power and defense are decided by "Special"

categories.desc: Attack moves of Normal, Fighting, Poison, Ground, Flying, Bug, Rock, and Ghost
